trial_name: OMEGA — Enteral Omega-3 Fatty Acid, γ-Linolenic Acid, and Antioxidant Supplementation in Acute Lung Injury (2011)
citation: Rice TW, Wheeler AP, Thompson BT, deBoisblanc BP, Steingrub J, Rock P, et al; National Heart, Lung, and Blood Institute Acute Respiratory Distress Syndrome Network of Investigators. Enteral omega-3 fatty acid, γ-linolenic acid, and antioxidant supplementation in acute lung injury. JAMA. 2011;306(14):1574-1581
trial_type: RCT — multicenter, double-blind, placebo-controlled, factorial with EDEN feeding trial
one_liner: In early acute lung injury (ALI)/ARDS, twice-daily bolus enteral supplementation with omega-3 fatty acids, γ-linolenic acid (GLA), and antioxidants resulted in fewer ventilator-free days and a mortality signal favoring control, leading to early trial termination for futility.

pico.population: Mechanically ventilated adults with early ALI (within 48 hours of meeting criteria) receiving enteral nutrition
pico.intervention: Twice-daily enteral bolus (120 mL each, total 240 mL/day) containing EPA 6.84 g, DHA 3.40 g, GLA 5.92 g, plus antioxidants (vitamin C 1000 mg, vitamin E 440 IU, beta-carotene 4.8 mg, zinc 24.2 mg, selenium 85.2 µg, L-carnitine 180 mg, taurine 350 mg), delivered alongside standard non–omega-3 enteral feeding
pico.comparison: Twice-daily isocaloric/isovolaemic control bolus (474 kcal, 22 g fat, 51.8 g carbohydrate, 20 g protein, no EPA/DHA/GLA, lower micronutrient doses), identical in appearance and smell
pico.outcome: Ventilator-free days (VFDs) from day 1 to day 28

background.existing_knowledge: ALI/ARDS is characterized by neutrophilic lung inflammation, permeability oedema, and prothrombotic signalling. Omega-3 fatty acids (EPA/DHA) may shift eicosanoid mediators toward less inflammatory profiles; GLA and antioxidants have anti-inflammatory/antioxidant effects. Prior small RCTs of enteral formula enriched with these nutrients reported improved oxygenation and other outcomes, but were limited by small samples and as-treated analyses. Observational data suggested low n-3 levels in ALI.
background.knowledge_gap: No large, blinded, intention-to-treat RCT had confirmed the efficacy and safety of such supplementation in ALI/ARDS.
background.hypothesis: Enteral bolus supplementation with EPA/DHA, GLA, and antioxidants would increase ventilator-free days to day 28 compared with an isocaloric control supplement.

methods.design: Randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled, multicentre trial within the NHLBI ARDS Network, conducted in factorial design with the EDEN feeding trial (trophic vs full-calorie); enrolled 2 Jan 2008 to 21 Feb 2009, stopped early at first interim analysis for futility after 272 participants.

inclusion: Within 48 hours of meeting ALI criteria
Bilateral infiltrates consistent with pulmonary oedema
No clinical evidence of left-sided cardiac failure
Clinical intent to provide enteral nutrition
exclusion: Severe chronic lung disease (n=500 screened excluded for this reason)
Time window exceeded (ALI >48 h or intubated >72 h; n=445)

methods.intervention: Twice-daily enteral bolus of 120 mL (total 240 mL/day) providing EPA 6.84 g, DHA 3.40 g, GLA 5.92 g, vitamin C 1000 mg, vitamin E 440 IU, beta-carotene 4.8 mg, zinc 24.2 mg, selenium 85.2 µg, L-carnitine 180 mg, taurine 350 mg. Started within 6 h of randomisation, continued until the earliest of 21 days, 48 h of unassisted breathing, or extubation. Background non-omega-3 enteral feeding via a protocolised algorithm.
methods.comparison: Twice-daily isocaloric/isovolaemic control bolus (240 mL/day: 474 kcal, fat 22 g, carbohydrate 51.8 g, protein 20 g, EPA/DHA/GLA 0 g, vitamin C 76 mg, vitamin E 12 IU, zinc 5.6 mg, selenium 18 µg, L-carnitine 38 mg, taurine 138 mg). Identical appearance, smell, and background feeding protocol.
methods.blinding: Double-blind; participants, clinicians, investigators, outcome assessors masked. Randomisation by central web-based system stratified by hospital and baseline shock.
methods.sample_size_power: Planned 1000 patients; 90.7% power to detect 2.25-day increase in VFDs (assumed mean 14, SD 10.5) with two-sided alpha 0.05, beta 0.093, using group sequential design with asymmetric efficacy/futility boundaries. Stopped at first interim analysis for futility after 272 randomised (143 intervention, 129 control).
methods.primary_outcome: Ventilator-free days (VFDs) from day 1 to day 28
secondary_outcomes: Days without nonpulmonary organ failure (circulatory, coagulation, hepatic, renal) to day 28
Plasma EPA levels (pharmacodynamic assessment in first 60 patients)
methods.follow_up: To day 60 or hospital discharge; primary endpoint assessed to day 28. Complete follow-up on all 272 participants.

headline_bullets: Trial stopped early for futility after 272 patients; primary analysis intent-to-treat.
Ventilator-free days significantly fewer with intervention: 14.0 vs 17.2 days (difference −3.2, 95% CI −5.8 to −0.7, P=0.02).
Mortality direction favored control: 60-day unadjusted mortality 26.6% vs 16.3% (difference 10.3%, 95% CI 0.7 to 19.9, P=0.054).
Diarrhoea more frequent with intervention: 29% vs 21% (P=0.001).
Pharmacodynamic separation confirmed: plasma EPA rose from ~0.5% to ~3.5% in the intervention group by day 3, unchanged in control.

outcomes_table.note: Negative value indicates fewer VFDs with intervention. Trial stopped for futility.
Early stopping limits precision; not adjusted for multiplicity.

subgroup_table.note: No evidence of interaction with feeding strategy on primary outcome.

safety: No other specific adverse events reported; trial stopped early.

domains.notes: Central web-based randomisation with stratification by hospital and baseline shock; concealed allocation.
Double-blind; intervention and control boluses identical in appearance and smell. Outcomes largely objective (VFDs, ICU-free days, mortality).
Complete follow-up to day 60/hospital discharge for all 272 participants; only 1/143 intervention patients received no n-3 doses. ITT analysis.
Mean receipt of 85% of planned bolus doses in both groups; background ventilation and fluid protocols standardised; bolus given even when continuous feeds interrupted.

Groups broadly similar (APACHE III, aetiology), but small imbalances: minute ventilation 11.4 vs 10.6 L/min (P=0.04); trend toward higher pre-study fluid intake 5085 vs 4387 mL (P=0.09) – may have favoured control.

internal_validity.verdict: Moderate to strong: strong randomisation, blinding, objective outcomes, and complete follow-up support validity, but early termination, non-inert control macronutrient composition, and baseline imbalances reduce confidence in precise effect estimates.

domains.notes: Typical early ALI/ARDS population from 44 hospitals; common aetiologies: pneumonia (52%), sepsis (23%). Excluded many with severe chronic lung disease, delayed presentation, or severe comorbidities – may not represent frailer or late-presenting patients.

Findings apply to twice-daily bolus supplementation dissociated from background feeds in protocolised, well-resourced ICUs. Extrapolation to continuous immunomodulatory enteral formulas or parenteral lipid emulsions is uncertain.

external_validity.verdict: Moderate: results are broadly applicable to early, mechanically ventilated ALI/ARDS patients receiving enteral nutrition in well-resourced ICUs, but may not fully generalise to different formulations, continuous delivery, or late-phase ARDS.

strengths: Randomised, double-blind, multicentre design with concealed allocation and excellent follow-up.
Protocolised co-interventions (ventilation, haemodynamics/fluid, glucose targets) reduced confounding.
Demonstrated pharmacodynamic separation (plasma EPA increased ~8-fold), confirming exposure.
Novel bolus strategy allowed intention-to-treat assessment despite feeding interruptions.
limitations: Stopped early for futility after 272/1000 participants, reducing precision and stability of estimates (especially mortality).

Intervention and control boluses were isocaloric but not macronutrient-matched; control provided more protein (20 g/day vs 3.8 g) and carbohydrate, complicating attribution to omega-3/GLA/antioxidants vs nutritional composition.
Bolus delivery of high-fat supplement may increase diarrhoea (29% vs 21%) and may not reflect continuous immunomodulatory formulas used in earlier trials.
P values were not adjusted for multiple comparisons or early stopping.

critical_appraisal.summary: Despite strong internal validity, early termination and the macronutrient mismatch between intervention and control boluses reduce confidence that the observed harm is solely attributable to omega-3/GLA/antioxidants; the signal of worse outcomes nevertheless refutes benefit from this specific bolus strategy in early ALI.
strengths: Double-blind RCT with complete follow-up and protocolised care.
weaknesses: Early stopping for futility renders effect estimates unstable.
Control group received substantially more protein and carbohydrate, creating a nutritional confound.
Bolus delivery caused GI intolerance and may not be comparable to continuous infusion.

sections.authors_conclusion: Twice-daily bolus enteral omega-3 fatty acid, GLA, and antioxidant supplementation did not improve clinical outcomes in early ALI and was associated with fewer ventilator-free days, potentially indicating harm; routine use is not recommended.

clinical_bottom_line.verdict: Do not routinely use this specific bolus omega-3/GLA/antioxidant supplement in early ALI/ARDS; it may cause harm (fewer VFDs, possible mortality increase).
clinical_bottom_line.applies_to: Mechanically ventilated adults within 48 hours of ALI onset receiving enteral nutrition in well-resourced ICUs.
clinical_bottom_line.does_not_mean: These findings do not necessarily apply to continuous enteral immunomodulatory formulas, parenteral omega-3 lipids, or different patient populations (e.g., late-phase ARDS).
implementation_caveats: Bolus delivery of high-fat supplements may increase diarrhoea and could reduce tolerance.
The macronutrient profile difference between the omega-3 and control boluses (protein, carbohydrate) is a major confound; separating the effect of omega-3s from overall nutrition is difficult.
Prior small trials using continuous formulas suggested benefit, highlighting that delivery strategy and comparator choice matter.

controversies.notes: Stopping at 27% of planned enrolment reduces precision; the nominally significant morbidity endpoints and mortality trend must be interpreted with caution given multiple endpoints and early stopping (editorial emphasised this).

Earlier small RCTs of continuous immunomodulatory enteral formulas reported improved oxygenation and outcomes. Discrepancies may stem from bolus vs continuous delivery, dissociated feeding design, macronutrient differences, and patient selection.

The control bolus provided ~16 g/day more protein and substantially more carbohydrate; these differences could independently affect outcomes, making it unclear whether harm is due to omega-3s or to relative protein/energy delivery.

Subsequent systematic reviews and meta-analyses have reported mixed findings; some suggest improved oxygenation or shorter ventilation with omega-3 formulas, but mortality effects are inconsistent and influenced by trial selection and small-study effects.
Guidelines cite OMEGA as a key negative multicentre trial and do not recommend routine enteral omega-3/GLA/antioxidant-enriched formulas or supplements in ARDS outside trials.

context_related_trials.trial: EDEN (Trophic vs Full-Calorie Feeding in ALI)
context_related_trials.relation: Conducted in factorial design with OMEGA; tested the effect of initial trophic vs full-calorie enteral feeding. No interaction between feeding allocation and omega-3 supplementation on VFDs (interaction P=0.47), indicating the OMEGA findings were independent of feeding strategy.

unresolved_questions: Would continuous infusion of omega-3 fatty acids (vs bolus) produce different outcomes?
Is there a subgroup (e.g., more severe hypoxaemia, sepsis) that might benefit from such supplementation?
What contribution did the large protein and carbohydrate differences between groups make to the outcome?
Can the harm signal be replicated or refuted in a fully macronutrient-matched trial?
What is the role of omega-3 fatty acids in parenteral nutrition for ARDS?

quick_recall.one_line_takeaway: In early ALI/ARDS, twice-daily bolus omega-3/GLA/antioxidant supplementation worsened ventilator-free days and trended toward increased mortality; it should not be used routinely.
